title: Runtime instrumentation delegator and header canonicalizer
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: Provide a small, runtime-attached instrumentation delegator that normalizes inbound outbound trace headers, exposes a compact SDK hook for language runtimes, and enforces an async-context leak guard for background fibers. This ticket implements the core runtime component and SDK connectors for Node and Go.

Motivation: We continue to see noisy trace fragments and header permutations across clients (legacy B3, OTTraceparent variants, custom x-redwood-* headers). That leads to orphaned spans and incorrect parentage in the console. A lightweight delegator that canonicalizes headers and offers a single low-cost callsite hook will reduce tracing discontinuities and make sampling deterministic across edges.

Scope and deliverables:
- Core runtime delegator: request-level component pluggable into the HTTP/gRPC edge and worker runtimes that inspects, normalizes, and emits a canonical trace envelope into the request context. Must be <50ns median additional overhead on hot path in optimized builds.
- Header canonicalizer: mapping table for common header formats (traceparent, b3, x-redwood-trace) with deterministic merging rules and collision resolution.
- SDK connectors: Node and Go adapters that read the canonical envelope and populate SDK-local context (no global state mutation).
- Async leak guard: best-effort detector that flags contexts that escape expected lifetimes (promises, goroutines) and emits a low-sampled debug span attached to the originating request for investigation.
- Sampling policy orchestrator (alpha): a pluggable hook that upstream services can query to reconcile sampling decisions (priority sampling hints from clients vs local budget).
- Compatibility: must interoperate with OpenTelemetry headers and be toggleable per-route with a config flag.

Non-goals:
- Full OTEL SDK replacement or opinionated sampling policy rollout.
- Language ecosystems beyond Node and Go in this phase.

Implementation notes and trade-offs:
- We prefer a delegator that operates on a canonical, minimized envelope rather than mutating raw headers to keep the wire-layer stable and reduce header churn. This avoids breaking downstream legacy consumers that rely on older header names.
- To keep overhead low we perform header parsing lazily: only when a hook is registered or when sampling/trace-id resolution is required. For typical non-traced requests the fast-path will inspect only a single header fingerprint and return.
- Leak detection will be heuristic: we will only emit a debug span when an escape pattern is observed twice from the same callsite in staging. The guard must never block request completion.
- We will implement the canonicalizer mapping as an ordered list of matchers with deterministic precedence; this makes rollbacks and audits straightforward at the cost of a small memory table.

Acceptance criteria:
- Delegator integrated at the HTTP edge and gRPC worker entry points and enabled by default for staging.
- End-to-end tests demonstrating header normalization from B3 + traceparent + x-redwood to a single canonical trace id in Console for synthetic workloads.
- Perf measurements showing median per-request overhead <50ns and 99th <300ns on our standard benchmark harness for hot-path requests (no hooks attached).
- Leak guard firing in staging with actionable debug spans (and a dashboard surface) when heuristics detect escapes.
- SDK connectors for Node and Go available as small packages and documented with quickstart snippets.
- A migration doc describing how to interpret original header values in audit logs for customers that need it.

Dependencies:
acceptance_criteria: Canonical trace envelope visible in Console for test requests that send mixed headers
Perf: median added latency <50ns on hot path, 99th <300ns (benchmark harness)
Node and Go SDK connectors published internally and integration test passing
Leak guard emits debug-span and corresponding alert in staging; false positive rate tolerable
Feature toggles exist per-route and are respected by Dedicated/Private deployments

2025-02-16 - QA (Lena Morozova): Added test cases for mixed header orders and duplicate trace ids — found collision handling ambiguity, PR updated to pick highest-sampled id.
2025-02-18 - Security (Ravi Singh): Reviewed mapping table; recommended adding an allowlist for incoming header sizes and a rate limit for debug-span emissions. Not blocking.
2025-02-19 - Marco Gutierrez: Opened PR #8214 with core delegator + Node connector. Addressed collision rule and added basic leak-guard heuristics. Requesting review from runtime and SDK owners.
2025-02-20 - Design (Priya Nair): Confirmed UX for sampling hint surfaced in Console. Suggested adding a human-readable audit of original headers in the trace view. Adding as follow-up.
2025-02-20 - Marco Gutierrez: Marking as In Progress. Next: finalize Go connector, add canary rollout, create dashboard for leak guard signals.
test_plan: Unit tests for header canonicalizer mapping rules (corner cases + collisions)
Integration tests: Node/Go connector end-to-end with Ingest and Console
Perf: run benchmark harness at 10k rps to measure median/99th overhead with no hooks
Canary rollout to staging with gradual ramp and leak-guard alerting enabled
Post-deploy: 48h observability sweep and manual trace audits for escaped contexts
notes: If perf targets are missed we'll convert header fingerprinting to a single-byte marker injected by the edge proxy as an opt-in optimization (requires proxy change).
We should coordinate with Dedicated product to expose per-customer toggle for leak-guard debug-span sampling rate.
Follow-up: evaluate adding Rust and Python connectors in next cycle based on usage metrics.
